Application
HTTP, FTP, DNS, SMTP, TLS, JSON. User-facing software, data formatting, encryption, sessions.
Transport
TCP (reliable), UDP (fast). End-to-end delivery and flow control.
Internet
IP, ICMP. Addressing and routing across networks.
Network Access
Ethernet, Wi-Fi. MAC addresses, framing, bits on the wire.
OSI is the common language for troubleshooting ("a layer 7 issue"). TCP/IP is what the Internet actually runs. Your API tests live at layer 7.

Safe, idempotent, state-changing: three different questions
The Web and HTTP
27
Safe
GET · HEAD · OPTIONS
Read-only. Never changes server data.
Idempotent
GET · HEAD · OPTIONS · PUT · DELETE
Repeat it: same end result as calling it once.
State-changing
POST · PUT · PATCH · DELETE
Creates, updates or removes data on the server.
POST · Not idempotent
POST /users {"name":"Asha"}
→ 201 Created id: 43
POST /users {"name":"Asha"}
→ 201 Created id: 44
Two records, two IDs. State grows with every call.
PUT · Idempotent
PUT /users/42 {"name":"Asha"}
→ 200 OK (replaced)
PUT /users/42 {"name":"Asha"}
→ 200 OK (same result)
Changes state once; repeating it changes nothing more.
PATCH · Generally not idempotent
PATCH /users/42
{"$inc":{"login_count":1}}
→ login_count: 5 → 6 → 7
(set email twice = same)
Depends on the operation: an increment compounds.
Test it: send the call twice, then compare the end state, not just the status code. ("Stateful" here means "changes server data"; HTTP itself is still stateless.)

Stateless protocol, stateful data: resolving the paradox

POST /accounts → A
GET /accounts/9 → B
Stateless = each request-response is independent and self-contained. The server keeps no memory of earlier requests.
So every request carries what the server needs: token, cookie or parameters.
Scalability
No per-user conversation to hold in memory. Free resources after each request.
Load balancing
A and B are interchangeable: any server handles any request.
Reliability
A dropped connection leaves no half-open conversation hanging.
Protocol (network layer): The channel keeps no session memory. Stateless.
Application (database layer): Data changes and persists: profile saved, payment recorded.
The server updates its database for one self-contained request, then forgets the conversation. Next: how apps add identity back.

Authentication vs authorization: who, then what
The Web and HTTP
31
Authentication: Who are you? → 401 Unauthorized
Authorization: What may you do? → 403 Forbidden
Basic auth
Base64 of user:password on every call
Authorization: Basic YWxpY2U6cGFzcw==
HTTPS only. Simple but weak.
API key
Secret string that identifies the calling app
x-api-key: 7f3a9c1e...
Identifies the app, not the user.
Bearer token (JWT)
Signed token: header.payload.signature. Server keeps no session
Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...
Readable (encoded, not encrypted). Has an expiry.
OAuth 2.0
Delegated access, e.g. "Sign in with Google". Access + refresh tokens, scopes
POST /oauth/token → access_token
A way to get tokens, not a token format.
Test list: no token (401) · expired token (401) · tampered token (401) · valid token, wrong role or scope (403) · another user's data (403/404).

Each HTTP version fixed the last one's bottleneck
The Web and HTTP
34
HTTP/0.9 · 1991
One-shot fetch
FIXED
Browser can ask for a document:
GET /index.html
NEW BOTTLENECK
Text only. No headers, no status codes (no 404). Connection closed after every reply.
HTTP/1.0 · 1996
Multimedia update
FIXED
Headers + status codes: images via Content-Type, errors via 200 / 404
NEW BOTTLENECK
A new TCP connection for every file: page, each image, CSS, script.
HTTP/1.1 · 1997
The workhorse
FIXED
Keep-Alive reuses one connection. Host header: many sites on one IP
NEW BOTTLENECK
Head-of-line blocking: requests queue one by one. Browsers open ~6 connections to cope.
HTTP/2 · 2015
Speed & parallelism
FIXED
Multiplexing: many streams on one connection. HPACK shrinks headers
NEW BOTTLENECK
TCP head-of-line blocking: one lost packet freezes every stream.
HTTP/3 · 2022
Ditch TCP for QUIC
FIXED
QUIC over UDP: only the hit stream pauses. Faster handshake, TLS built in
NEW BOTTLENECK
Newest: adoption still growing (details on next slide).
WHAT'S NEXT
QUIC tuning: better congestion control for 5G, satellite, moving vehicles
WebTransport: low-latency, two-way, multi-stream on HTTP/3 (WebSockets successor)
AI-aware priority: research: favour live audio over background prefetch
QUIC: the engine under HTTP/3
The Web and HTTP
35
HTTP/2 stack
HTTP/2
TLS (encryption)
TCP (reliability)
IP
HTTP/3 stack
HTTP/3
QUIC: streams + TLS 1.3 + loss recovery
UDP
IP
Same HTTP on top (methods, status codes, headers). Only the transport underneath changed.
1
Independent streams
A lost packet pauses only its own stream. Others keep flowing. (Fixes TCP head-of-line blocking.)
2
Faster connections
Transport + TLS handshake combined into one step (1-RTT). Returning visitors: 0-RTT.
3
Connection migration
Connection ID instead of IP + port: Wi-Fi to mobile data without dropping the session.
QUIC = from Google, standardised by the IETF (RFC 9000). Testers: if UDP is blocked, clients fall back to HTTP/2 over TCP, so test both paths.

Today: HTTP/1.1, 2 and 3 all run side by side
The Web and HTTP
37
HTTP/1.1
Legacy fallback
Universal fallback for older clients, proxies and legacy internal services.
HTTP/2
Current workhorse
Most major sites, CDNs (Cloudflare, Akamai) and clouds. Carries the bulk of browsing today.
HTTP/3
Modern standard
Growing fast: Google, YouTube, Meta and Cloudflare serve a large share over QUIC/UDP. On by default in Chrome, Safari, Edge, Firefox.
WHY NOT 100% HTTP/3 YET?
Server & network infrastructure
Older servers, firewalls and enterprise networks may block or misconfigure UDP, forcing fallback to TCP (HTTP/2 or 1.1).
CPU overhead
Processing UDP/QUIC takes slightly more server CPU than TCP. Hardware offload and optimisation are closing the gap.
Tester tip: clients fall back silently, so a test can pass over HTTP/2 while HTTP/3 is broken. Test each version where it matters.

40 years of APIs: what it was, how it worked, the catch
From web pages to APIs
40
Era
What it was
How it worked
The catch
1980s RPC
"Pretend the remote server is local"
Remote Procedure Call: the first attempt to run code on another computer.
Call a function as if it lived on your machine, though it ran across the network.
Locked to specific languages and hardware. C server + Fortran client = broken.
1991 CORBA
"Universal enterprise heavyweight"
Common Object Request Broker Architecture: one standard so any language talks to any language.
A central broker plus rigid interface files translate calls between systems.
Bloated, hard to set up, a nightmare through firewalls. Buckled under its own weight.
1998 XML-RPC
"Let's use the web instead"
CORBA stripped down to standard HTTP plus XML text.
Wrap the function call in an XML document and send it as an HTTP POST.
XML is verbose and heavy. Proved HTTP was the right transport; needed a sturdier framework.
1998-2000 SOAP
"Corporate enterprise standard"
Simple Object Access Protocol (neither simple nor object-based): XML-RPC plus thousands of pages of rules.
Built-in security, transaction guarantees and auto-generated contracts (WSDL).
Bureaucratic: a simple lookup needs a block of boilerplate XML. Symbol of over-engineering.
2000 REST
"Back to simplicity"
Roy Fielding's style: copy how the real World Wide Web works.
Everything is a resource (noun). Use HTTP verbs: GET reads, POST creates, DELETE removes. Light JSON or XML.
WHY IT WON: intuitive, human-readable, scales easily. Backbone of public web and mobile APIs.
2015 GraphQL
"Ask for exactly what you want"
Facebook's fix for REST over-fetching (too much data) and under-fetching (too little).
Client sends a query describing the exact JSON shape it wants. Server returns only that.
Pushes query parsing and optimisation onto the server. Caching is trickier than REST.
2015 gRPC
"High-speed internal microservices"
Google's modern RPC, built for speed and backend systems.
Compact binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2. No human-readable text at all.
WHERE IT SHINES: internal microservices. Rarely used where humans must read the traffic.
Each step fixed the pain of the one before it. The pendulum swings between powerful-but-heavy and simple-but-limited.

Naming rule: URLs are nouns (/users), never verbs (/getUser, /deleteUser). The HTTP method carries the verb.
2000-2014: how REST quietly took over
From web pages to APIs
44
2000
Salesforce & eBay launch early web APIs
mostly XML / SOAP
2002
Amazon Web Services
APIs as a product
2004-06
Flickr, then Twitter APIs
simple URLs + data
2006
Amazon S3
REST over HTTP in the cloud
~2006
JSON overtakes XML
lighter, readable
2007
iPhone
mobile apps need light APIs
2011-14
Netflix & co. split monoliths
"Microservices" named (2014)
2015
Swagger becomes OpenAPI
a standard contract for REST
The recipe that made REST win: simple HTTP + JSON + mobile + cloud. Testers: this is why almost every API you test today looks like this.
Why REST won: the advantages
From web pages to APIs
45
🧩
Simple & familiar
Uses plain HTTP verbs and URLs everyone already knows
📖
Human readable
JSON, easily tested with a browser or a tool
📈
Scales easily
Stateless: add more servers behind a load balancer
⚡
Cacheable
Reuse responses; less load, faster
🌍
Language neutral
Java, .NET, JS, Python, mobile: all speak HTTP
🔌
Loosely coupled
Client and server evolve independently
Honest trade-offs: no built-in strict contract (use OpenAPI), can be chatty, over- and under-fetching of data.
Richardson Maturity Model: how RESTful is your API?
From web pages to APIs
46
Level 3
Hypermedia (HATEOAS)
Responses include links to next actions
Level 2
HTTP verbs + status codes
GET/POST/PUT/DELETE and 200/201/404 (most real APIs)
Level 1
Resources
Many URLs: /users/42, /orders/7
Level 0
One endpoint (RPC)
Everything is POST /service
{ "id": 42, "name": "Asha",
"links": { "self": "/users/42", "orders": "/users/42/orders" } }
OpenAPI: the contract for a REST API
From web pages to APIs
47
openapi: 3.0.3
info: { title: User API, version: 1.0.0 }
paths:
/users/{id}:
get:
summary: Get one user
parameters:
- { name: id, in: path,
required: true,
schema: { type: integer } }
responses:
'200': { description: OK }
'404': { description: Not found }
Documentation
Interactive docs (Swagger UI) that always match the API
Mock server
Frontend and testers start before the backend exists
Code generation
Client and server stubs in many languages
Validation
Check real requests and responses against the contract
Contract-first
BA, dev and QA agree the file before code is written
History: Swagger (2011) → OpenAPI Initiative (2015) → OpenAPI 3.0 (2017) → 3.1 (2021). Ask for the OpenAPI file before you start testing.
REST in the real world: what testers hit first
From web pages to APIs
48
Versioning
/v1/users vs /v2/users
TEST: Old version must keep working. Check breaking changes.
Pagination
GET /users?page=2&size=20
TEST: Test first, last, empty and out-of-range page; max size.
Rate limiting
429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
TEST: Exceed the limit, then confirm the reset and the header.
Idempotency
POST /payments
Idempotency-Key: 9b1c...
TEST: Retry the same call: one charge, not two.
Quick win: add 429 Too Many Requests and 401/403 checks to every API test pack, not only 200 and 404.
REST's pain points led to GraphQL (2015)
From web pages to APIs
49
REST: 3 calls, lots of unused data
📱 App
GET /users/42
GET /users/42/orders
GET /orders/7/items
GraphQL: 1 call, ask only for what you need
📱 App
POST /graphql
{ user(id: 42) {
name
orders { id total }
} }
{ "data": { "user": { "name": "Asha",
"orders": [ {"id":7,"total":99} ] } } }
•Pros: no over/under-fetching, one endpoint, strongly typed schema
•Cons: harder caching, server complexity, often 200 even on errors (check the "errors" field)
gRPC (2015): fast, typed, service-to-service
From web pages to APIs
50
// user.proto (the contract)
service UserService {
rpc GetUser (UserRequest) returns (User);
}
message UserRequest { int32 id = 1; }
message User {
int32 id = 1;
string name = 2;
}
Service A
(Java)
Service B
(Go)
binary messages over HTTP/2
•Contract first (.proto), code generated
•Binary = smaller and faster than JSON
•Streaming both ways
•Weak in browsers; hard to read by eye
Rule of thumb: REST for public/partner APIs, gRPC for fast internal calls, GraphQL for flexible client-driven UIs.
After gRPC: the evolution went sideways, not forward
From web pages to APIs
51
Connect-RPC
gRPC for the browser
THE PROBLEM
Browsers cannot speak full gRPC without a heavy proxy (Envoy): no low-level HTTP/2 control.
WHAT IT IS
gRPC-style code with Protocol Buffers over plain HTTP/1.1, 2 or 3 as normal fetch calls (JSON or binary). Popular 2022-24.
Browser → Connect → gRPC backend
WebTransport
WebSockets' successor
THE PROBLEM
WebSockets suffer TCP head-of-line blocking, a poor fit for real-time media and games.
WHAT IT IS
Browser API on HTTP/3 + QUIC: two-way, multi-stream, low-latency. Gaming, live audio/video, collaborative canvases.
Browser ⇄ HTTP/3 (QUIC) streams
GraphQL Subscriptions & Federation
the graph grows up
THE PROBLEM
One frontend needs data from hundreds of independent microservices.
WHAT IT IS
Subscriptions push live updates. Federation stitches many services (often gRPC underneath) into one graph.
Frontend → one graph → many services
THE ECOSYSTEM TODAY
Public web & mobile APIs
REST and GraphQL remain dominant
Internal microservices
gRPC: undisputed king for speed and binary efficiency
New additions
Connect-RPC (gRPC everywhere) and WebTransport (browser streaming)
Real-time and push: polling, webhooks, SSE, WebSockets
From web pages to APIs
52
Polling
client asks again and again
Client → "anything new?"
Client ← "no"
(repeat every few seconds)
USED FOR
Simple dashboards, status checks
TEST NOTE
Wasteful: most answers are 'no'
Webhook
server calls YOUR URL on an event
Server → POST /my-hook
{"event":"payment.ok"}
USED FOR
Payments, Git pushes, alerts
TEST NOTE
Need a receiver or mock to capture calls
SSE
one-way stream, server to browser
Client → GET /events
Server ⇒ data… data…
text/event-stream
USED FOR
Live scores, notifications, feeds
TEST NOTE
Check reconnect and event order
WebSocket
two-way, always-on connection
GET /chat Upgrade: websocket
101 Switching Protocols
Client ⇄ Server
USED FOR
Chat, trading, collaboration
TEST NOTE
Test drops, reconnect, ordering
Beyond one request, one response: you must test connection, message order, reconnects and timeouts, not just a status code.

PART 5
Microservices
How modern systems are built, and where REST fits
Monolith vs microservices
Microservices
56
Monolith
Users
Orders
Payments
Catalog
🗄️ One database
Microservices
Users service
🗄️ own DB
Orders service
🗄️ own DB
Payments service
🗄️ own DB
Catalog service
🗄️ own DB
•Monolith: simple start; one change = redeploy everything; hard to scale parts
•Microservices: small, independent, own data; scale and release separately; more moving parts
How REST holds microservices together
Microservices
57
🌐 Web app
📱 Mobile app
🤝 Partner
🚪 API Gateway
auth · routing · rate limits
Users service
🗄️
Orders service
🗄️
Payments service
🗄️
📨 Message broker (async events)
REST calls = synchronous request/response
Events = fire and forget, processed later
REST is the common language between clients and services, and often between services too. That is why API testing is the heart of microservice quality.
Events and message brokers: asynchronous services
Microservices
58
Synchronous: REST calls
Orders
Payments
Inventory
Caller waits for each answer. If one is down, the whole chain fails.
Asynchronous: events
Orders
(producer)
Message broker
Kafka · RabbitMQ
"OrderPlaced"
Payments
Inventory
Email
Producer publishes and moves on. Consumers process when ready.
Use REST when…
you need an immediate answer: get a user, check a price, validate a coupon.
Use events when…
work can happen later or many services care: order placed, send email, update analytics.
New test cases: duplicate, out-of-order and delayed messages, retries, and "eventually consistent" data. Wait or poll for the result; never use fixed sleeps.
What microservices mean for testers and BAs
Microservices
59
UI tests
few, slow, brittle
API / service tests
many, fast, stable ← the sweet spot
Unit tests
most, fastest
Mocks & stubs
Fake a dependency that is slow, unavailable or must fail on demand
Contract tests
Provider and consumer agree on the message shape
Resilience cases
Timeouts, retries, 5xx from a dependency
Observability
Trace IDs across services to find the failing hop
New risk categories: partial failure, version mismatch, data consistency between services. Test them at the API layer.

Wrap-up
What this means for your role, and where to go next
What to take away, by role
Wrap-up
61
Manual testers
•Read a raw HTTP request and response
•Check status code, headers and body
•Try missing/invalid tokens, bad input, repeated calls
Automation engineers
•Automate at the API layer: fast and stable
•Chain calls to cover business flows
•Mock dependencies; add contract tests
Business analysts
•Describe resources, rules and error cases
•Agree status codes and field rules up front
•Think contract first (OpenAPI)
In one sentence: protocols are contracts; HTTP is the common language of the web; REST is the way we use HTTP to expose business resources; microservices are many small RESTful services.

Metadata about the message
Idempotent

Stateless

Lightweight text data format

Standard way to describe a REST API
Gateway
Single front door to many services
